subject: health
unitTitle: Substance Use, Community Risk, and Harm-Reduction Literacy
title: Guided practice: harm-reduction concepts and the arguments made for and against them
focus: harm-reduction concepts and the arguments made for and against them
essentialQuestion: What does the evidence say actually reduces harm, and what only sounds tough?
keyPoints: Harm reduction aims to reduce injury or death among people who may continue a risky behavior; evaluating it requires evidence, goals, limits, and implementation context.
Use observable facts, reliable information, and the appropriate support route; do not infer a person’s health, motives, or character from one detail.

For harm-reduction concepts and the arguments made for and against them, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support.
privacySafeScenario: Evaluate two fictional community prevention campaigns against stated evidence criteria, then redesign the weaker one and state how its effect would be measured.
studentTask: Apply the lesson facts to a supplied fictional case about harm-reduction concepts and the arguments made for and against them. Produce a three-part response that identifies the key concept, chooses a safe and feasible action, and explains the choice with two details from the instruction plus an appropriate support route.
knowledgeCheck: In two or three sentences, explain the most important distinction in harm-reduction concepts and the arguments made for and against them; use one lesson fact and name the evidence, safety check, or support route that makes the explanation dependable.
completionCriteria: The response completes every named part of the harm-reduction concepts and the arguments made for and against them task using the supplied fictional or public case.
The response uses at least two accurate details from the lesson instruction and distinguishes evidence from assumption.
The response gives a safe, feasible next step or support route and does not depend on private disclosure, body comparison, or recorded media proof.
adaptationChoices: Evaluation and redesign may be written, storyboarded, dictated, or completed on a supplied criteria template.
extensionChallenge: Apply harm-reduction concepts and the arguments made for and against them under a new constraint, compare two approaches, or explain the idea to someone else with an original fictional example, without completing another learner's graded work.
accessibilitySupports: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.
Evaluation and redesign may be written, storyboarded, dictated, or completed on a supplied criteria template.
trustedAdultNote: This course teaches health information and does not diagnose; direct urgent safety or health concerns to a trusted adult or qualified professional.

optionalReflection.prompt: Invite the learner to notice one safe, optional example of harm-reduction concepts and the arguments made for and against them in daily life. No purchase, account creation, photograph, recording, or private disclosure is required.

neverRequires: This task never requires body weight, height, BMI, or body-fat percentage.
This task never requires calorie counting or a diet or weight-loss goal.
This task never requires disclosing private medical history, a diagnosis, or sexual history.
This task never requires a photograph, video, or voice recording of the learner as proof.
This task never requires a public performance or an audience.

contentProvenance.objective: Explain harm-reduction concepts and the arguments made for and against them accurately using current, reliable health information rather than assumption or anecdote.
